[1] For our first two winters in Bergen, my sister Paz did all of our talking. She was fourteen when we arrived and had learned more Norwegian on the plane, my father liked to say, than he learned in the whole first year. Paz talked to the bank. Paz talked to the woman at the pharmacy who wanted to know whether our mother's pills were for the heart or for the blood. Paz talked to the landlord, Mr. Haugland, a tall man with a soft voice who called every problem in the building "a small thing."

[2] I was eleven, and I understood more than anyone gave me credit for, mostly because no one asked. I sat at the edge of those conversations the way you sit at the edge of a pool you have been told is too deep, and I kept a tally of the words I knew. By the second winter the tally was long enough that I had started to notice something I did not have a name for. What Mr. Haugland said and what Paz told my father he had said were not always the same length.

[3] In February the radiator in the room I shared with Paz began to knock all night and give off no heat. Paz was in Trondheim with her class for four days. My father looked at the radiator, looked at me, and put on his coat.

[4] "You come," he said in Spanish. "You will help."

[5] Mr. Haugland lived on the ground floor behind a door with a brass nameplate he polished himself. He listened to my father's three sentences of Norwegian, which my father had practiced in the stairwell, and then he turned to me, because everyone in that building had learned to turn to a child.

[6] "Tell your father it is a small thing," he said. "The pipes are old. The plumber comes for the whole building in March, and he will look at it then. Until then I can lend you a heater. And tell him, please, that I have mentioned the cooking smells in the hall before. Some of the neighbors have said something."

[7] I turned to my father. I had every word. I could feel them lined up in my mouth like coins, and I knew exactly what each one was worth, and I knew, too, what the last ones would do to his face. He had cooked for us every night since our mother went into the hospital in the autumn. The smell in the hall was his sofrito, the same one he had made in Valparaíso, and it was the one thing in that country he had not had to learn.

[8] "He says the plumber will come in March," I said in Spanish. "He says the pipes are old. He says he will lend us a heater until then."

[9] My father nodded and thanked Mr. Haugland, and Mr. Haugland looked at me for a moment longer than he needed to. Then he went to find the heater.

[10] Paz came home on Sunday and a paper bag of brown cheese for my father, who disliked it and ate it anyway. That night, under the new heater's orange coil, I told her what Mr. Haugland had said, all of it, and what I had said, which was less.

[11] I expected her to be angry. For two winters she had been the one who carried the words, and I had taken them and dropped some on the floor. Instead she was quiet for so long that I thought she had fallen asleep.

[12] "The pharmacist," she said finally. "Last year. She said the pills were very strong and that Mamá's doctor should have called us weeks before. I told Papá she said they were strong." She turned over toward the wall. "You have to decide which half you are going to carry. Nobody tells you that part. You just find out you have been deciding."

[13] I had thought, all that winter, that Paz's job was to be a kind of pipe, the words going in at one end and coming out unchanged at the other. In Mr. Haugland's doorway I had been proud of having every word, as if that made me a better pipe than she was. Now I saw that she had been holding every word too, for two years, and setting some of them down where no one would trip on them, and that the setting down was the work.

[14] In the morning my father made sofrito, and the smell went up the stairwell the way it always did, and I did not say anything about it, and neither did Paz.

passage_title: The Stone at the Bottom of the Sea
passage:
[1] On Yap, a small group of islands in the western Pacific, there are stones that no one would mistake for coins. The largest of the carved limestone discs called rai stand taller than a person and weigh several tonnes; the smallest could be carried under one arm. Each has a hole bored through its centre, so that a pole could be passed through it and the stone lifted by a team of men. Many of the big ones have not moved in a century. They lean against houses and line village paths, and yet they change hands.

[2] The limestone did not come from Yap. Yapese voyagers quarried it on the islands of Palau, several hundred kilometres to the southwest, shaped it there, and brought it home by canoe and raft across open ocean. A stone's worth depended on its size and the quality of its working, but also on its story: how hard it had been to get, who had brought it, and whether lives had been lost on the voyage. Two stones of the same diameter could be worth very different amounts.

[3] What happens when a large stone is given in a marriage exchange or to settle a dispute is, to an outsider, almost nothing. The stone stays where it is. What changes is what everyone knows about it. Its new owner does not need to see it, or even live near it, because the community remembers who owns it, and that shared memory is the stone's title.

[4] The most famous illustration was recorded by the American traveler William Henry Furness III, who visited Yap around the start of the twentieth century. He was told of a family whose wealth included an enormous stone that none of them had ever seen. Generations earlier, a raft carrying it home from Palau had been caught in a storm, and the crew had cut it loose to save themselves. When they reached shore they testified to its size and quality and to the fact that it had been lost through no fault of the owner. Their account was accepted, and the stone at the bottom of the sea went on being counted, and spent, like any other.

[5] Economists have loved this story for a long time, because it seems to show something that ordinary coins disguise. A coin looks as if its value is inside it. The stone at the bottom of the sea plainly has nothing inside it that anyone can use; what it has is a reputation and an agreement. On this reading, money was always a kind of record of who is owed what, and the metal or paper or limestone is merely the place the record happens to be kept. Gold bars that change owners inside a vault without ever leaving it are, in this view, the same arrangement with a heavier door.

[6] The story is a good one, and the lesson is not wrong, but anthropologists who have worked on Yap tend to add a warning. Rai were never everyday money. People did not buy fish or taro with them. The stones passed between families and villages on large occasions, such as marriages, funerals, and the settling of quarrels, and they carried obligations and histories that a dollar does not carry. A coin is useful precisely because any one is as good as any other. A rai stone was valued for the opposite reason: no stone was quite like another, and the history attached to each was part of its value rather than a description of it.

[7] The point shows most clearly in what happened in the late nineteenth century, when an Irish-American sea captain named David O'Keefe began carrying stones from Palau to Yap aboard his ship, cut with iron tools, in exchange for copra and sea cucumbers. He brought a great many. By most accounts, the stones he delivered were valued below those brought home in the old way, because they had cost their owners so little danger. If rai had been simply a record of quantity, more stone would have meant more money. Instead, stones without a story were worth less.

[8] Whether this makes Yap a lesson about all money or an exception to it depends on which feature one decides is essential. The economist keeps the record and lets the stone go. The anthropologist notices that, on Yap, the record could not be separated from the stone it was written on, and that the people who used the stones took care to remember both.

[1] When Ruth Askel began designing houses in the river towns of the upper Midwest in the early 1950s, the hallway was the first thing she removed. Her clients were young families buying their first houses on modest lots, and Askel argued that a corridor was the most expensive room in a house that no one ever lived in: forty or fifty square feet of floor whose only job was to keep the other rooms from touching. In her houses the rooms touched. You came in through the kitchen, passed through the living room to reach the bedrooms, and found that the two smaller bedrooms opened onto each other.

[2] She was not naive about what this cost. In a talk to a builders' association in 1956 she said that a hallway "buys the right to walk past one another," and that a family which has paid for that right will use it. Her houses declined to sell it. A teenager going to bed passed through the room where her parents were reading; a father coming home late crossed the kitchen where someone was still doing homework. The plan made encounters that a corridor would have prevented, and Askel meant it to.

[3] Critics at the time called the houses cramped, and a few later owners did wall off a passage. The criticism misses what the plans achieve. The sixty-odd Askel houses still standing are remarkable less for their size than for how generous they feel: with no hall eating the floor, every room is a little larger than the matching room in the houses beside it, and light from the south windows reaches the back of the house unblocked. Askel's own phrase for the result was "a house that cannot be lonely." It remains the best description of her work anyone has offered, and it applies to the families as much as to the rooms.

Passage B

[1] I grew up in an Askel house in Orrin Falls, the third of four children. My parents bought it in 1961 from its first owners, who had added nothing to it but a coat of paint, and I can confirm that it could not be lonely. It also could not be private, and the second fact shaped our family more than the first.

[2] Because every route through the house crossed some other room, we learned early to read the house as a timetable. My older brother did not walk through the living room after nine if our parents had friends over; he climbed out his window and came round to the kitchen door. My mother hung a curtain across the arch to the bedrooms, then a second one, and by the time I was ten there were four curtains in a house designed to have no barriers at all. We called them by name. Drawing "the blue one" meant that whatever lay behind it was not to be walked through, and everyone respected it, because everyone needed the same respect in return.

[3] I do not think the house made us closer, exactly. I think it made us skilled. We became expert at being in the same room without being together: reading with our backs to one another, conducting whole arguments in lowered voices, waiting at the edge of a doorway until a conversation reached a place where it could be interrupted. Visitors from houses with hallways found us oddly formal. We were not formal. We were negotiating, constantly, over something the plan had refused to give us, and we had become very good at it.

[4] When I read the praise of these houses now, I recognize the light and the extra floor, both of which are real. What I do not recognize is the idea that an encounter the plan forces on a family is the same as one the family chooses. Askel removed the hallway. She did not remove the need it had served. She only moved it out of the walls and into us.

[1] The Venus flytrap grows wild in only one small region of the world: the boggy coastal plain of North and South Carolina, where the soil is wet, sandy, and so poor in nitrogen that most plants struggle there. The flytrap makes up the difference by eating animals, mostly ants, spiders, and beetles that wander across its leaves. The prey supplies what the soil does not. Each trap is a single leaf folded into two lobes and fringed with stiff bristles, and on the inner face of each lobe stand a few trigger hairs, usually three, each about as long as an eyelash.

[2] Touch one of those hairs once and nothing visible happens. Touch it, or another hair on the same trap, a second time within roughly half a minute, and the lobes swing together in a fraction of a second, one of the fastest movements known among plants. Wait too long between touches and the first one is forgotten; the trap stays open, and the count starts over.

[3] That rule makes sense once you consider what a false alarm costs. Closing is expensive. A trap that has shut on nothing needs the better part of a day to reopen, during which it catches nothing, and each trap can close only a limited number of times before it blackens and dies. A raindrop, a falling seed, or a blade of grass blown across the leaf will usually strike a hair once. An insect walking around the inside of the trap, hunting for the nectar that drew it there, will usually strike hairs again and again. Demanding a second touch screens out much of the weather while sacrificing very little of the food.

[4] The first closure is not the end of the decision. When the lobes first meet, they do not seal. The bristles along their edges interlock loosely, forming something more like a cage than a box, and a small enough insect can climb out between the bars. This, too, appears to be economical. Digesting a meal takes the trap a week or more, and a gnat would not repay the effort. What keeps the trap shut is the struggling of whatever is inside: each time the prey brushes a trigger hair it sends another signal, and as the signals accumulate the lobes press tight, seal their edges, and turn the trap into a closed stomach.

[5] In 2016 a team of plant biologists in Germany reported how far this counting goes. By stimulating trigger hairs mechanically and measuring the plant's response, they found that roughly five signals were needed before the trap began producing digestive enzymes in quantity, and that further signals raised production further. [3] That rule makes sense once you consider what a false alarm costs. Closing is expensive. A trap that has shut on nothing needs the better part of a day to reopen, during which it catches nothing, and each trap can close only a limited number of times before it blackens and dies. A raindrop, a falling seed, or a blade of grass blown across the leaf will usually strike a hair once. An insect walking around the inside of the trap, hunting for the nectar that drew it there, will usually strike hairs again and again. Demanding a second touch screens out much of the weather while sacrificing very little of the food.

[4] The first closure is not the end of the decision. When the lobes first meet, they do not seal. The bristles along their edges interlock loosely, forming something more like a cage than a box, and a small enough insect can climb out between the bars. This, too, appears to be economical. Digesting a meal takes the trap a week or more, and a gnat would not repay the effort. What keeps the trap shut is the struggling of whatever is inside: each time the prey brushes a trigger hair it sends another signal, and as the signals accumulate the lobes press tight, seal their edges, and turn the trap into a closed stomach.

[5] In 2016 a team of plant biologists in Germany reported how far this counting goes. By stimulating trigger hairs mechanically and measuring the plant's response, they found that roughly five signals were needed before the trap began producing digestive enzymes in quantity, and that further signals raised production further. The title of their paper said plainly that the plant counts. A large, strong insect that struggles for a long time sends many signals; a small one that soon gives up sends few. The trap, in effect, matches its investment to the size of its catch.

[6] It is tempting to say the plant knows how many times it has been touched, and botanists themselves use the word "counting." But nothing in the trap stores a number. The leading explanation is chemical. Each touch sets off an electrical signal that raises the level of calcium inside the trap's cells, and that level falls away again over the following seconds. One touch leaves the level below the point at which the trap fires. A second, arriving before the first has faded, pushes it over. Seen this way, the half-minute window is not a rule the plant follows but simply how long the first signal takes to disappear.

[7] That is a less romantic account than counting, but in one respect it is more impressive. A brain is an expensive organ, and the flytrap has none. It has arrived at a decision rule that sorts rain from prey, small prey from large, and promising effort from wasted effort, using nothing more than a signal that fades at the right speed.
